statements.text: AI tools tend to automate tasks within a job more often than they replace whole jobs.
statements.explanation: Most jobs are bundles of tasks, and a model handles some of them well, such as drafting, summarizing, and sorting. The judgment, relationships, and accountability parts stay with people. The practical question is which tasks to hand over, not whether a role disappears.

statements.text: AI makes everyone more productive by about the same amount.
statements.explanation: Measured gains vary widely by task, by person, and by how the tool is used. Routine writing tasks often speed up; tasks that need checking can slow down when the output is wrong. Expect uneven results and measure your own.

statements.text: Productivity gains from AI vary widely by task and by the person using it.
statements.explanation: Studies of AI at work find large gains on some tasks and none or losses on others. The difference often comes down to whether the person can judge the output quickly. Pick tasks where you can tell good from bad at a glance.

statements.text: A person plus an AI tool always outperforms either one working alone.
statements.explanation: Research on human-AI teams finds they sometimes underperform the better of the two, because people defer to the tool or the tool adds noise. The split of work matters. Teams do best when the person decides and the tool proposes.

statements.text: Human-AI teams sometimes perform worse than the person or the tool alone, depending on how the work is split.
statements.explanation: When a person rubber-stamps the tool, the pair inherits the tool's mistakes. When the tool handles a step the person was better at, quality drops. Assign the tool the parts it is reliable on and keep the final call human.

statements.text: A tool that is right nine times out of ten does not need its tenth answer checked.
statements.explanation: High reliability creates blind spots: the better a tool performs, the less people look, and the single wrong answer goes out unnoticed. Build a check that is cheap enough to run every time, such as a second source or a sample review.

statements.text: When a tool is right most of the time, people tend to stop checking it, and that is when errors get through.
statements.explanation: Automation bias is the habit of accepting a system's output because it is usually correct. The fix is a routine rather than vigilance: a checklist, a sample audit, or a rule that certain outputs always get a second look.

statements.text: The person who sends an AI-drafted email is still responsible for what it says.
statements.explanation: A tool cannot be held accountable; the sender can. Read every draft as if you wrote it, because to the recipient you did. This is the same standard that applies to a template, a spell checker, or a colleague's suggestion.

statements.text: If an AI-drafted document contains an error, nobody is accountable because a model wrote it.
statements.explanation: Accountability does not transfer to a tool. The person who sent it, and the organization behind them, own the result. That is why review before sending matters more, not less, when a model produced the first draft.

statements.text: Many employers publish a policy on which AI tools staff may use and with what kinds of data.
statements.explanation: The policy usually names approved tools, forbidden data such as customer records and credentials, and when disclosure is expected. If your workplace has one, it answers most day-to-day questions. If it has none, ask before pasting anything sensitive.

statements.text: Pasting customer or colleague data into a personal AI account can break company policy and privacy law.
statements.explanation: A personal account sits outside the organization's agreements and controls. Data about other people carries legal duties that do not pause because the tool is convenient. Use the approved tool, or remove the identifying details first.

statements.text: An AI tool approved for one kind of data at work is approved for every kind of data.
statements.explanation: Approvals are usually scoped: a tool cleared for public marketing copy may be barred from customer records or source code. The difference is in the contract and the data classification, not in the tool's abilities. Check the scope, not just the name.

statements.text: Buying an AI tool with a privacy certificate means the company using it is automatically compliant.
statements.explanation: The vendor's controls cover the vendor's side. The organization still decides what data goes in, who can use it, how outputs are reviewed, and how people are told. Compliance is a process the buyer runs, with the tool as one part.

statements.text: Some fields and employers expect you to say when AI helped produce a piece of work.
statements.explanation: Disclosure norms are spreading through academic rules, professional codes, publishing policies, and company handbooks. Praxis discloses its own AI use in its commit history. When in doubt, a short note on how the tool was used is cheap and builds trust.

statements.text: Keeping a note of which outputs were AI-assisted helps when a document is questioned later.
statements.explanation: If a figure or a claim is challenged, knowing which parts came from a tool tells you where to re-check first. Teams that track this can answer questions quickly and fix the process, not just the document.

statements.text: Tools that claim to detect AI-written text can say with certainty whether a colleague used AI.
statements.explanation: Detectors work on statistical patterns and produce both false alarms and misses, with higher false alarm rates for some writing styles and for non-native English writers. A detector score is a weak hint, not evidence about a person. Policies should rest on disclosure, not detection.

statements.text: A model can draft a first version of a routine document so a person spends their time on judgment and editing.
statements.explanation: First drafts of status updates, job descriptions, and standard replies are where models save the most time. The person adds the context the model lacks and removes what is wrong. The work shifts from typing to deciding.

statements.text: An AI summary of a long report contains everything that was in the report.
statements.explanation: Summaries drop material by design, and a model decides what to drop by what looks typical, not by what matters to you. Conditions, exceptions, and numbers are common casualties. Ask for the items you care about by name, then check them in the source.

statements.text: An AI summary can drop a condition or an exception that changes what a document means.
statements.explanation: A clause such as unless the contract was signed before a date can vanish from a summary and flip the meaning. Treat a summary as a map of where to read. Before acting, open the section the decision depends on.

statements.text: Meeting transcription tools capture every speaker correctly and never mix up who said what.
statements.explanation: Speaker labels are guesses from voice and timing, and they fail with crosstalk, similar voices, and room audio. Action items can land on the wrong person. Read the commitments back to the room or check them against your own notes.

statements.text: An AI meeting summary can assign a commitment to the wrong person, so the action list needs a check against the notes.
statements.explanation: The summary inherits any speaker mix-up from the transcript and then compresses it. Confirm owners and dates for each action before sending the summary. A thirty-second read-back prevents a week of confusion.

statements.text: Telling a model what role to take, such as a careful editor, shapes the tone and focus of its answer.
statements.explanation: Role prompting steers which patterns the model draws on: an editor role brings out concision and structure, a support agent role brings out warmth and steps. It is a framing tool, and the output still needs checking.

statements.text: Telling a model to act as an expert gives it the knowledge and judgment of an expert.
statements.explanation: A role changes style and emphasis, not what the model knows. It can sound like a specialist while making a beginner's mistake. For expert-level work, supply the facts, the standards, and the examples, and have a real expert review the result.

statements.text: A chatbot's confident legal, tax, or medical answer can be relied on as professional advice.
statements.explanation: The model has no license, no duty of care, and no knowledge of your situation beyond what you typed. It can give useful background and questions to ask. Decisions with legal, financial, or health consequences belong with a qualified person.

statements.text: A model does not know your organization's internal procedures unless they are given to it in the prompt or through retrieval.
statements.explanation: Internal documents are not in public training data. Without them the model produces a generic procedure that looks plausible and may contradict your real one. Paste the relevant section, or use a tool connected to your document store.

statements.text: A model knows your company's internal rules because it was trained on the whole internet.
statements.explanation: Internal handbooks, pricing rules, and workflows are not public, so the model never saw them. Asked anyway, it will produce a generic answer in a confident voice. Give it the actual document and ask it to work from that.

statements.text: Tasks with a clear right answer that is cheap to check are the best candidates for AI help at work.
statements.explanation: Reformatting a table, drafting a reply to a standard request, or converting units are quick to verify. Open-ended judgment calls are slow to verify and easy to get subtly wrong. Start where checking is fast and widen from there.

statements.text: Code or spreadsheet formulas written by a model need testing like any other code.
statements.explanation: A model produces code that runs and looks right far more often than code that is right. Run it on known inputs, check edge cases, and read it. The time saved on writing is partly spent on testing, and that trade is still a good one.

statements.text: Code written by a model does not need testing because the model has already checked it.
statements.explanation: A model can write code and a convincing statement that it works in the same breath, with no execution behind either. Testing is the only evidence. Treat model-written code exactly like code from a new colleague: review it and run the tests.

statements.text: AI tools at work are only useful for technical roles.
statements.explanation: The heaviest workplace uses are writing, summarizing, translating, planning, and answering questions, which cut across every role. Technical staff use the tools differently, not more legitimately. The skill that matters is clear instruction and careful review.

statements.text: An AI assistant can be given a whole process and left unsupervised once it has done it correctly a few times.
statements.explanation: A few good runs show the tool can do the task, not that it will do it every time on every input. Unusual cases are where it fails, and those arrive without warning. Keep a review step sized to the cost of a mistake.

statements.text: Models tend to agree with the view the user expresses, so asking for the strongest counterargument gets a more useful answer.
statements.explanation: This tendency is called sycophancy: a model echoes the framing it is given. At work it turns a brainstorm into an echo chamber. Ask what is wrong with the plan, or pose the question without revealing your preference.

statements.text: Asking a model to be objective is enough to get an unbiased answer.
statements.explanation: The instruction changes the tone, not the data the model learned from or the framing in your question. Bias shows up in which examples it picks and whose perspective it defaults to. Test with varied prompts and compare, rather than trusting a label.

statements.text: Using AI to screen job applications removes human bias because a computer has no opinions.
statements.explanation: A screening model learns from past hiring decisions, including their biases, and applies them at scale and without explanation. Several documented systems penalized candidates by gender or background. Human review and bias testing are expected, and in some places required.

statements.text: When a model helps screen job applications, its errors and biases affect many people at once, so testing and human review are expected.
statements.explanation: A single reviewer's bias touches the applications they read; a model's bias touches all of them. Organizations test such systems across groups, keep a person in the decision, and tell applicants when automated tools are used.

statements.text: A vendor's demo on clean sample files shows how the tool will behave on your real work files.
statements.explanation: Demos use tidy inputs chosen to succeed. Real files have scanned pages, inconsistent formats, missing fields, and jargon. Run a pilot on a sample of your own documents, including the ugly ones, before judging the tool.

statements.text: Writing a repeatable prompt template for a routine task makes the output more consistent across the team.
statements.explanation: A shared template fixes the format, the required fields, and the checks, so results differ by content rather than by who wrote the prompt. The Praxis Prompt Builder and Preflight Checklist exist for exactly this kind of standardization.

statements.text: Staff need no training to use AI tools well because the tools understand plain English.
statements.explanation: Plain English gets an answer; good results come from knowing what to include, what to leave out, how to check output, and when not to use the tool at all. Those are learnable skills, and teams that teach them get better and safer results.

statements.text: The more tasks you hand to a tool, the fewer skills you need to keep yourself.
statements.explanation: The skill to judge the output is what makes the tool safe to use, and it fades without practice. Keep doing some of the work by hand, especially the parts you review, so you can still tell a good result from a plausible one.

statements.text: The skills that matter most for AI at work are writing clear instructions, checking output, and knowing when not to use the tool.
statements.explanation: Specific prompts, a habit of verification, and a sense of which tasks fit are what separate good results from costly ones. These transfer across tools and model versions, while memorized prompt tricks go stale.
